title: 3D Genomics Analysis
introduction:
OpenPretext computes a set of analyses from the contact map: where contact drops across a position, how it falls with distance, and how the genome splits into two compartments. They are aids for finding places to look at. They are not measurements you can compare with published Hi-C figures, and this lesson explains why.

In this lesson, you'll learn to:
• Run the core analyses (insulation, P(s) decay, compartments)
• Know what the numbers are computed from, and what that limits
• Read the analysis tracks against the map
• Compare a P(s) curve before and after an edit
• Export analysis results for external use

We'll use the koala genome, which has a clean chromosome structure.

steps.title: Open the Sidebar
steps.instruction: First, open the sidebar by pressing **I** or clicking the **Info** button in the toolbar. Scroll down to find the **3D Analysis** section. It is organized into Compute, Results, and Export tabs. The analyses run automatically when the genome loads, so the Results tab opens showing them.
steps.hint: The 3D Analysis section is in the sidebar, below the History section.

steps.title: Run the Core Analysis Pipeline
steps.instruction:
The three core analyses run automatically when the genome loads, and the Results tab opens to show them. To run them again yourself, click the **Compute** tab, then **Compute All**. The three analyses are:

• **Insulation score**: how much contact crosses each position. Dips mark places where the two sides contact each other less, such as TAD boundaries and joins between sequences that do not belong together
• **P(s) decay**: how the map's values fall as two positions get further apart along a chromosome
• **A/B compartments**: the two groups of regions that contact their own group more than the other

All three run in a background Web Worker so the UI stays responsive.
steps.hint: The computation may take a few seconds. Buttons are disabled during computation to prevent conflicts.

steps.title: Know What the Numbers Are Computed From
steps.instruction:
Before reading any number, know what it is made of. A `.pretext` file does not hold contact counts. PretextMap, the program that writes the file, scales the rows, compresses the values, and adjusts the contrast so that the map is easy to read by eye. It does this separately for each zoom level.

What this leaves you with:

• **Reliable**: where things are. A dip in insulation, a change of compartment, a brighter or darker block
• **Reliable**: change on one map. If a curve or track moves after an edit, the edit moved it
• **Not reliable**: the size of a number. Slopes, ratios and scores computed here are not the quantities of the same name in Hi-C papers, and they should not be compared between genomes

The same is true of the picture itself: colours change when you zoom between levels, because each level has its own contrast. Compare brightness within one zoom level.
steps.hint: PretextView shows the same adjusted values, so the map looks the same there. The limit only matters when a number is taken from it.

steps.title: Understand the P(s) Decay Chart
steps.instruction:
In the Results tab, find the **P(s) decay chart**, a log-log plot of the map's mean value against distance along a chromosome. Below it, a second panel shows the local slope at each distance.

• The curve should fall as distance grows. A flat stretch or a rise is worth a look at the map
• The **exponent** is the slope of a straight line fitted to the curve, and **R²** says how well a straight line fits. On real maps the fit is often loose
• Neither number is the exponent reported in Hi-C papers, because the values are contrast-adjusted. There is no range the exponent should fall in

The chart is most useful for comparison. Click **Snapshot Baseline** to save the current curve. After curation, the new curve is drawn over the baseline so you can see what your edits changed.
steps.hint: On nine real maps the fitted exponent ran from about -0.65 to -1.90, and it changed by up to 1.1 for one file depending on the zoom level read. Use it for before and after, not as a grade.

steps.title: Examine Analysis Tracks
steps.instruction:
The analysis results are also rendered as **tracks** along the edges of the contact map. Toggle tracks on with **X** or the **Tracks** button. You should see:

• **Insulation Score** (green line): dips indicate TAD boundaries
• **TAD Boundaries** (red markers): detected boundary positions
• **A/B Compartments** (blue-yellow-red heatmap): blue = B (inactive), red = A (active)

If the assembly carries them (written by curationpretext, or computed from a loaded reference FASTA), you will also see the **curator tracks**: **Coverage**, **Gaps**, **Telomeres**, and **Repeat density**, the standard aids for finding where to look. A red **Weak joins** track marks contig junctions the Hi-C signal does not support.

Zoom into a chromosome to see how these tracks relate to the contact map structure.
steps.hint: Compare the insulation dips with the visual boundaries between bright contact blocks in the map.

steps.title: Balance the Rows
steps.instruction:
Some rows of a map are brighter than others overall. **Balance rows (ICE)** rescales rows and columns until their sums are even, which can make the compartment pattern easier to see.

Open the **Compute** tab, then click **Balance rows (ICE)**. After it completes, notice:
• A new 'ICE row factors' track shows how much each row was rescaled
• The P(s) curve and compartments are recomputed on the balanced map

With contact counts, this step corrects for sequencing bias. Here it works on values PretextMap has already scaled and contrast-adjusted, so treat it as another way of looking at the map, not as a correction.
steps.hint: ICE typically runs 10-50 iterations. Rows with very little signal are left out.

steps.title: Export Analysis Data
steps.instruction:
Analysis results can be exported for use in external tools (R, Python, IGV). Click the **Export** tab to find the export buttons:

• **Insulation (BedGraph)** loads in genome browsers
• **P(s) (TSV)** has distance and mean map value columns
• **Compartments (BedGraph)** holds eigenvector values

These files use genomic coordinates derived from your contig ordering and sizes. Anyone who uses them should know they come from contrast-adjusted map values.
steps.hint: BedGraph files can be loaded back into OpenPretext via the Load Track button to compare analyses across different sessions.

steps.title: Analysis Summary
steps.instruction:
You've learned the core analysis workflow:

1. **Compute All** runs insulation, P(s), and compartments
2. The numbers come from contrast-adjusted map values: positions and changes are reliable, sizes are not
3. **Analysis tracks** put the results beside the contact map so you can check each one by eye
4. The **P(s) chart** with a baseline shows what an edit changed
5. **Balance rows** gives another view of the map
6. **Export** saves results for external analysis

In your curation workflow, use the analyses to find places to look, and decide from the map. No single number here says whether an assembly is good.
